extracted.intended_audience: software developers and code reviewers using GitHub/merge requests (engineering teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for engineers performing peer code reviews on GitHub/merge requests, covering timeliness, tone, technical checks, and process hygiene to protect project quality and developer experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not harm the project’s code
rubrics_metrics.description: Overarching principle: the reviewer’s primary responsibility is to avoid introducing harm to the project via accepted changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reviewing as a responsibility toward the codebase and teammates; be picky for the right reasons. This principle motivates all the other best practices described in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect people’s time (respond promptly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start reviewing the code within two hours after its first submission when possible; avoid letting days or weeks pass before reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely reviews respect the submitter’s workflow and reduce costly context switches. Late reviews force authors to re-learn the feature and increase chance of errors. Be the most timely reviewer you can be; even small delays can waste significant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always provide constructive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Use positive, constructive language and remember there are humans behind the code; frame suggestions rather than orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer phrasing like "I suggest" or "You could improve X by doing Y." Avoid imperatives or harsh language such as "Do this" or "This is just wrong." Be mindful of how written comments can be interpreted; aim to encourage authors so mistakes are less likely to be repeated. The article gives concrete examples contrasting unkind vs constructive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your ego out of code reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote a culture where the best argument wins; avoid assuming seniority implies correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support opinions with reasons, links to docs/articles, or examples rather than feelings. If discussions get heated, schedule a call to discuss constructively. Stay firm when appropriate but be open to learning; the goal is the best outcome for the project, not personal victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about what needs to be improved
rubrics_metrics.description: Make comments clear, grammatically unambiguous, and point to the exact line or location being discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check your wording and grammar to avoid confusion. Specify which function/class/line you're referring to—don't rely on ambiguous pronouns. If you include code in a comment, make it readable and clear enough to communicate your intent. Ambiguous comments force unnecessary clarifying questions and waste time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t just hope for the code to work (verify by testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check out the branch locally, ensure the project builds, and test the changes yourself; do not rely solely on the author’s claim that it works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate functionality, exercise edge cases, and intentionally try to cause errors. Two minds (author + reviewer) reduce bugs. Ensure everything builds before testing. This increases confidence and catches issues automated tests may miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforce code submission best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage authors to adopt practices that make reviews easier and safer (CI, code coverage, PR templates, frequent small commits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable continuous integration so automated tests run on PRs, use code coverage tools to show test coverage, and maintain a well-written PR template to remind submitters to describe changes and request particular reviewer attention. Frequent commits and CI reduce merge conflicts and debugging time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be strict about temporary code
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat code marked as "temporary" with the same rigor as permanent code; temporary fixes tend to become long-lived technical debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not relax testing, review, or quality standards just because a change is labelled temporary. Enforce discipline consistently to avoid accumulating dirty legacy code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check the project’s satellite files
rubrics_metrics.description: Review related non-code artifacts that should change with code (documentation, tests, configuration, build files, changelog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that tests were added or updated for new features, documentation and build files reflect refactors, and the changelog accurately records operations. Satellite files are as important as code for project health and maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the bigger picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how a change integrates into the larger system: maintenance burden, scalability, and future readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the change benefits the project long term, whether it will scale, and whether peers (including future-you) can read and understand it months from now. Use these considerations to inform the approve/reject decision—PRs are part of a broader system, not isolated edits.
